section.title: Introduction to Algorithmics
section.content: Algorithmics is the science of designing and studying algorithms. Designing an algorithm to solve a problem is synonymous with proposing a method for automatic resolution of said problem. Therefore, algorithmics is considered one of the essential elements of computer science, as automatic information processing cannot exist without algorithmics.

bulletPoints.point: ▶️ Algorithmics studies the design and analysis of algorithms
▶️ An algorithm is an ordered list of primitive operations called instructions
▶️ Each instruction is an action applying a defined operation to one or more data items
▶️ Algorithmics is indispensable for automatic information processing

section.title: Steps of Automatic Problem Resolution
section.content: In computer science, automatic problem resolution is carried out by following 4 essential steps: Problem → Analysis → Algorithm → Programming → Execution. The Analysis step consists of understanding the problem by answering three fundamental questions.

bulletPoints.point: 📋 Analysis: study and understand the problem (What data do we have? What results do we want? What processing should be done?)
📋 Algorithm: write the solution in the form of an algorithm
📋 Programming: translate the algorithm into an executable program (programming language)
📋 Execution: introduce the program into the computer and observe the results

section.title: Notion of Algorithm and Structure
section.content: An algorithm is an ordered list (or set) of primitive operations, called instructions, performing specific processing for solving a problem. The name algorithm comes from the mathematician Abou Jaafar Mohamed Ibn Moussa Al Khawarizmi. A basic algorithm generally comprises 4 parts.

bulletPoints.point: 📋 Header: begins with the word ALGORITHM followed by the algorithm name
📋 CONSTANT (or CONST): declaration of algorithm constants
📋 VARIABLE (or VAR): declaration of algorithm variables
📋 Body: between BEGIN and END, contains the list of sequential instructions
▶️ Each instruction ends with a semicolon (;)
▶️ Instructions are executed sequentially from BEGIN to END

section.title: Simple Data Types in Algorithmics
section.content: A type determines the set of values that a data item can take. A type is characterized by its values and the operations that we can perform on data having this type. The simple data types in algorithmics are: Integer, Real, Character, String, and Boolean.

bulletPoints.point: 🔢 Integer (Int): indivisible quantity (set Z), represented on 16 bits (2 bytes). Example: -5, 15, 30
🔢 Real (Float/Double): fractional value (set R), represented on 4 or 6 bytes. Example: -15.5, 3.75, -2.62
🔢 Character (Char): any keyboard symbol (space, letters, digits, special characters), represented on 1 byte. Example: 'a', 'B', '7'
🔢 String (String): sequence of characters, maximum 255 characters, each character on 1 byte. Example: 'COMPUTER SCIENCE DEGREE'
🔢 Boolean (Bool): two logical values only — TRUE or FALSE
🔢 Warning: a Character data item must be between single quotes. A designates a name, 'A' designates the letter A

section.title: Forms of Simple Data in Algorithmics
section.content: Simple data to be processed by the instructions of an algorithm can be: a constant, a variable, or an expression. A constant has a fixed name, a fixed type and a fixed value. A variable has a fixed name, a fixed type, but a modifiable value.

bulletPoints.point: 💻 Constant: value that cannot be modified during execution. Declaration: CONSTANT identifier = Value; (in C: int identifier = Value;)
💻 Variable: value that can be redefined at any time. Declaration: VARIABLE list_of_identifiers : TYPE; (in C: TYPE list_of_identifiers;)
▶️ Identifier: alphanumeric name starting with a letter, without special characters, unique in the algorithm, different from keywords
🧮 Arithmetic expression: form X OP Y where OP ∈ {+, -, *, DIV, MOD, /}. Example: 2 * X + Y
🧮 Boolean expression: can be a relational expression (>, <, ≥, ≤, =, ≠) or a logical expression (AND, OR, NOT)
💾 In reality, a variable or constant is a memory space. At any given moment, a variable contains only one value

section.title: Permitted Operations on Basic Types
section.content: Each basic type has a set of operations that can be applied to data of that type. The order of evaluation of expressions follows priority rules.

bulletPoints.point: 🧮 Integer: addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), integer division (DIV), remainder (MOD), comparisons (<, ≤, >, =, ≠)
🧮 Real: addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), real division (/), remainder (MOD), comparisons (<, ≤, >, =, ≠)
▶️ Character: comparisons only (<, ≤, >, =, ≠)
▶️ String: concatenation (+ or &), comparisons (<, ≤, >, =, ≠)
🧮 Boolean: conjunction (AND), disjunction (OR), negation (NOT)
🧮 Operator priorities: 1-NOT, -(unary) | 2-*, /, DIV, MOD, AND | 3-+, -(binary), OR | 4-<, <=, =, >, <>
🧮 Parentheses are evaluated first; at equal priority, evaluation is from left to right

section.title: Basic Instructions of an Algorithm
section.content: In an algorithm, we distinguish two types of instructions: processing instructions (perform operations) and control instructions (indicate the manner in which operations are performed). The three basic processing instructions are: read, write, and assignment.

bulletPoints.point: 🧮 READ (scanf): assigns a value entered from the keyboard to a variable. Syntax: READ(v1, v2, ..., vn); — Impossible to read a constant or an arithmetic expression
📤 WRITE (printf): displays results on screen. Syntax: WRITE(v1, v2, ..., vn); — Can display variables, constants and expressions
✏️ Assignment (<-): gives an existing value in memory to a variable. Syntax: Variable_Name <- value; — The value can be a constant, a variable or an expression
▶️ Real <- Integer is allowed | Integer <- Real is not allowed
▶️ String <- Character is allowed | Character <- String is not allowed
📥 READ operation: program stops → keyboard input → storage in memory → execution resumes

section.title: Execution Trace of an Algorithm
section.content: The execution trace allows you to follow the course (manual execution) of an algorithm step by step, instruction after instruction, to ensure its correct functioning. It is presented in the form of a table.

bulletPoints.point: 💻 Verify the values of variables after execution of each instruction
▶️ Ensure that the algorithm terminates
▶️ Ensure that the result produced is correct
📤 Example: ALGORITHM Trace — VAR X, Y, Z : Integer — X<-3 ; Y<-7 ; Z<-X ; X<-Y ; Z<-Z+1 ; WRITE(2, X, Y) → displays: 2 7 7 ; WRITE(X+1/2) → displays: 7.5
💻 In the trace, we follow column by column the variables and the screen at each instruction

section.title: Complete Example: Average Calculation Algorithm
section.content: Write an algorithm that calculates a student's average in computer science for EMD1, going through the analysis step. The formula is: Average = (EMD_Grade * 2 + Evaluation_Grade) / 3.

bulletPoints.point: 📋 Analysis — Inputs: EMD_Grade, Evaluation_Grade
📋 Analysis — Outputs: Average
📋 Analysis — Processing: (EMD_Grade * 2 + Evaluation_Grade) / 3
📋 Algorithm: ALGORITHM studentAverage ; VAR Evaluation_Grade, EMD_Grade, Average : Real ;
📋 Body: READ(Evaluation_Grade) ; READ(EMD_Grade) ; Average <- (EMD_Grade * 2 + Evaluation_Grade)/3 ; WRITE(Average) ;

section.title: Best Practices and Points of Vigilance
section.content: A few essential rules to remember for correctly designing and writing algorithms according to the ALSD course from Béjaïa.

bulletPoints.point: ✔️ An algorithm is built BEFORE writing a program
▶️ In algorithmics, not all data is of the same nature (False: different types exist)
▶️ The READ instruction is a processing instruction (True), but not IF...ELSE
✏️ You cannot assign a value to a constant (neither with READ nor with assignment)
✔️ An identifier must be alphanumeric, start with a letter, without special characters, unique and different from keywords
✔️ To declare the constant X=2: CONST X=2; right after the algorithm header

subsection.title: Exemple de trace d'un algorithme
subsection.content: Que sera-t-il affiché à l'écran par l'algorithme suivant :

Trace d'exécution :
- Après X<-3 : X=3, Y=?, Z=?
- Après Y<-7 : X=3, Y=7, Z=?
- Après Z<-X : X=3, Y=7, Z=3
- Après X<-Y : X=7, Y=7, Z=3
- Après Z<-Z+1 : X=7, Y=7, Z=4
- ÉCRIRE(2, X, Y) affiche : 2 7 7
- ÉCRIRE(X+1/2) affiche : 7.5
